chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 81 to 100: short poems of hill courtship and its dangers (the night path, the town's talk, the friend testing and pressing the girl), set beside wives waiting through the rain season, a husband's go-between mocked, and a foster mother who reads her daughter's flight too late. Puram names (Aay's Pothiyil, Anji's raids, the Kolli of Porayan and of Ori) are used as measures for private feeling.

81.reading: The friend tells the lover that the girl, who believed her word because it carried his, now sits alone in a corner under the many-branched njaazhal with its fresh buds, her new beauty gone; then she points: look over there and keep it in mind, our small good town of drooping palmyras, where the sea of smelling waves and the shore grove show side by side like moonlight and darkness.
81.nuance: The friend admits her own part: the girl yielded because the friend's word stood surety for his (நின்சொற் கொண்ட என்சொல்). Pointing out the town and its landmarks is a way of telling him where to come openly, that is, to ask for her.

thinai_evidence.note: shore grove, njaazhal and palmyra are neythal things; the colophon's kurinji has no support in the poem

comparisons.tenor: the pale sea and the dark grove seen together

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she calls him நின் and speaks of the girl as இவள்; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

82.reading: The woman asks her friend what sort of man he is, the one who used to stroke her long curled hair, hold her and wipe her weeping eyes saying 'do not cry', and who has not come back in the bitter-dew season, when the plump avarai creeper flowers on the second-sown millet of the hill farmer's wide field.
82.nuance: The tender gestures she recalls are his own, so the question 'who will wipe my eyes?' is also an accusation: the comforter is the cause. The avarai flowering on the millet's second sowing dates the broken promise on the field itself.

thinai_evidence.note: she waits past the season he named, which is mullai's situation, though every thing in the poem is of the hills

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி)

83.reading: The friend blesses the mother: may she win the world of great name with rare ambrosia for her food, because she said that the lord of the high hill, where sweet jackfruit hang from every branch like one's own food eaten in one's own house, will come.
83.nuance: The blessing is extravagant (the gods' food, the world above) for a single sentence, 'he will come'; the size of the gratitude shows how long the waiting has been. The simile of eating one's own food in one's own house anticipates the household the coming promises.

thinai_evidence.note: the jackfruit hill and its lord fix the hill country

comparisons.tenor: the jackfruit hanging ripe and sweet on their own branches

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem; she reports the mother's words to the girl

84.reading: The foster mother recalls that when she turned the girl over to embrace her, the girl said 'I am sweating'; only now does she understand that it was distress; yet that girl, fragrant with the vengai and kaanthal of Aay's cloud-crept Pothiyil, was cooler to the touch than the water-lily.
84.nuance: The last line undoes the first: the girl was cool by nature, so the 'sweat' was an excuse to slip the embrace of the woman who raised her, already turned toward another. The foster mother's memory of her daughter's fragrance is all hill-country flowers, the lover's land.

thinai_evidence.note: the foster mother reads the sign only after the girl has gone, the paalai situation of the elopement

comparisons.tenor: the girl's coolness to the touch

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks her discovery aloud, and the girl's going is inferred from the colophon's paalai

85.reading: The friend says that the lord of the rich town, where the hopping sparrow cock of the village plucks the scentless white flowers of the sweet-jointed sugarcane to line a nest for his hen near her laying, is sweeter than anyone and full of great love: in his bard's mouth.
85.nuance: The praise collapses on its last word, வாயே: the great love exists in the bard's telling. The sparrow's flowers are scentless (நாறா); whether that is a further slight on the husband's gifts is doubtful and not tagged.

thinai_evidence.note: the sugarcane and the lord of the rich town are marutham's

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the bard comes as the husband's go-between; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

iraicchi.act: the sparrow cock gathers cane flowers to build a nest for his hen as her laying nears
iraicchi.sense: even a village sparrow provides for his mate in her time, while the husband's care for his wife exists only in the bard's words

86.reading: Her red-streaked cool eyes overflowing like a breached dam, sick with an unbearable illness and shaken by loneliness, the woman asks whether anyone else is listening, at midnight in the cold season when the north wind flings the heavy rain, to the thin, poor voice of the curved bell with its tongue that clangs each time the lonely cow stirs.
86.nuance: 'Does anyone else hear?' means 'is anyone else awake?': the only other wakeful thing is a cow whose loneliness (புலம்பு) rings out in the same word the poem uses for hers (புலம்பலை).

thinai_evidence.note: the cold season and the midnight watch are kurinji's time

comparisons.tenor: her tears overflowing like water breaking a dam

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

87.reading: The woman says people hold that the fearsome old god in the kadamba tree of the village common destroys the false; her hill lord is not false in the least; yet her forehead has paled with longing and her broad soft shoulders have grown slack as his care slackened.
87.nuance: She clears him before the god so the god will not strike him for a broken oath; but the punishment the poem shows has landed on her own body, so the defence carries its own accusation. The doubled verbs (பசைஇப் பசந்தன்று, ஞெகிழ ஞெகிழ்ந்தன்று) tie each loss to his loosening.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill country of the lover fixes the land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

88.reading: The friend tells the girl that the lord of the high hill of loud white waterfalls comes even at midnight across the hard slope where the small-eyed great tusker, struck by a strong tiger, loses its old fierceness; and they, for their part, will not shrink from the shame of scandal.
88.nuance: The last line can be read as resolve (we will not let fear of talk keep him in danger: the love should be made known and the marriage pressed) or as a reckless 'we are past caring for blame'. The tusker that loses to the tiger shows what the path can do even to the strongest; it carries the danger, not an act of the lovers, so it is scene.

thinai_evidence.note: waterfall, tusker and tiger are the hill's things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

89.reading: Strangers sing the open-mouthed pounding song at their broad-footed mortars and nobody minds; what harm can come to this foolish town if this soft young girl, like the lovely figure that the dark-eyed goddess drew on the western face of fearsome Kolli of Porayan of the great ornaments, sang as she pounded?
89.nuance: The friend's point is the double standard: the same pounding song is harmless in strangers' mouths, but from this girl it is taken as a sign (presumably because she sang of the lover's hill). The town is called பேதை, the word usually given to an innocent girl.

thinai_evidence.note: the town's talk about an unmarried girl's song is the secret love of kalavu; the poem has no fields or ford for the colophon's marutham

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of the town in the third person, perhaps for the lover or the mother to hear

90.reading: The friend exclaims to the girl: what a thing it is! the friendship of the hill lord, from whose slopes where pepper vines climb, after the dark rain-cloud has thundered all night and fallen, the falls carry down to the drinking ford a fragrant jackfruit that a shaggy stag touched and loosened, has wasted your soft shoulders and yet has brought forth your constancy.
90.nuance: A near miss for ullurai: the fruit that the stag loosens and the stream carries to a common ford invites a mapping (the girl won by the lover, then exposed to everyone), but the poem never anchors a second correspondence, so the scene stays scene. சால்பு is given a double edge: the friendship 'yielded' wasting and, with it, endurance.

thinai_evidence.note: pepper slopes, stag and jackfruit are kurinji things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

91.reading: The woman tells herself that if she is to be the wife of the lord of the cool ford, where kendai fish in the deep pool snap at the ripe striped fruit of the tangled rattan, then let the cares in her heart be many and her nights of sleep few, like those of a town on the deadly frontier at night that fears Anji of the tall chariot and hard-driving elephants, whose hand gives like unceasing rain.
91.nuance: A near miss for ullurai: fish snapping at whatever fruit drops into the pool can be read as the husband taking every woman who comes his way, but the poem never states his straying, so there is no anchor. The wife's curse on herself borrows its measure from war: her marriage will be a frontier town under raid.

thinai_evidence.note: the pool, its fish and the lord of the cool ford are marutham's

comparisons.tenor: her own nights of little sleep as the husband's wife

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses herself in the second person (நின் நெஞ்சு, நீ துஞ்சு நாள்); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

92.reading: The woman says the curve-winged birds in the wide sky where the sun has set are to be pitied: carrying food to push into the mouths of their young in the tall kadamba beside the path where they roost, they hurry on their way.
92.nuance: Her pity for the birds is pity for herself turned outward: their haste home at dusk with food for their young is what her own man does not show. The birds are the whole poem, so striking them leaves nothing; it fails the deletion test and is not tagged iraicchi.

thinai_evidence.note: the sunset hour is neythal's time

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

93.reading: The woman tells her friend not to speak against him even if her fine beauty fades, she wastes away and her sweet life leaves her: is he not mother and father to them? and what is sulking worth when love is gone?
93.nuance: Two refusals in four lines: she will not let the friend blame him, because he is her whole family; and she will not sulk, because sulking presumes a love that would notice it. The second refusal is the bitterer.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem turns on whether to sulk against an erring husband, marutham's situation

comparisons.tenor: the husband, on whom she depends wholly

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி), who urges her to quarrel; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

94.reading: The woman tells her friend that the buds of the foolish pitthikam, deceived by the great cold rains, have reddened even earlier than before, and she is bewildered: what will become of the man who left her, if he too hears alone at midnight the thunder of the massed storm clouds that shakes the great hill of waterfalls?
94.nuance: The bud is 'foolish' for blooming to rains that are not the promised season, and she half admits she is like it. Her fear is turned toward him: she imagines him, not herself, alone under the thunder.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season of waiting is mullai's time

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

95.reading: The man says that the grace of the broad-shouldered young daughter of the hill farmer of the small hamlet, on the flowered slope where the pure white falls from the great hill brim in the rock hollows, is like water, and it has put out his strength, which was like fire.
95.nuance: The two similes are one action: water does not defeat fire by being stronger but by being what fire cannot survive. Softness (சாயல்) is set against will (உரன்), and the soft wins.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill farmer's daughter on the slope fixes the hill country

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the companion is inferred: the man answers a reproach for his changed state; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

96.reading: The woman says to her friend: you ask 'what can I do about the lord of the great hill of waterfalls and vengai trees?'; if I had not taken that as a joke, what would have become of you, fine-browed one?
96.nuance: The friend's question tests her (shall I refuse him?); the woman answers that she chose to hear it as a joke, and that if she had taken it seriously the friend would have had to answer for the consequence. Who would suffer, and how, is left unsaid.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill of waterfalls and vengai names the lover's land

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (நன்னுதல்); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

97.reading: The woman says she is here; her beauty is there in the shore grove with an unending sickness; the lord of the shore is in his own town; and their secret, turned to open talk, is out in the common square.
97.nuance: Four things in four places: herself, her beauty (left where they met), him, and the secret. The love has come apart into its parts, and the only part that has gone public is the talk.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore grove and the lord of the shore fix the coast

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

98.reading: The woman tells her friend it would be good if they could find someone who would go close to him, carrying a few flowers of the rainy-season peerkam that grows thick in the wet green bushes of their garden, and tell him 'the fine-browed one has become like this'.
98.nuance: The message is the flower: the yellow peerkam, held up with 'she has become like this', shows her pallor without a word of complaint. That it is the rain-season flower also reminds him that the season of his return has come.

thinai_evidence.note: the rain-season flower and the waiting at home are mullai's

comparisons.tenor: her pallor, shown by the yellow flower held up with 'like this'

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she names the friend (தோழி); the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

99.reading: The man says: did I not remember? remembering, did I not think hard? thinking, was I not bewildered? but such is the way of the world, and my great desire held back to the end, like the flood that once touched the branches of the tall kadamba and has sunk until one must scoop it to drink.
99.nuance: The three questions climb (remember, think, be bewildered) and each takes the last verb as its start. The flood simile can be read two ways: his desire was once as high as the treetops and shrank under duty, or it was a flood he held back to the last; the sense of மீண்டு கடைக்கொள is not certain.

thinai_evidence.note: the man, back from his duty, answers whether he remembered her while away

comparisons.tenor: his great desire held in check by duty

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he answers a charge of forgetting, most likely put by the friend; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

100.reading: The man says that the girl of the kaanthal-fenced hamlet, where people sow mountain rice on the spread of the falls, weed out the broad-leafed kulavi and the green maral, and when hungry trade the tusks of fierce elephants for food, has the innocence of the figure on the western face of Kolli of Ori of the strong bow, and her broad shoulders, like bamboo, are hard to win.
100.nuance: The girl comes from a hamlet that lives by elephant tusks, yet she is as unknowing as a painted figure; the hardness of her people's life and her innocence make her hard to win.

thinai_evidence.note: mountain rice, kaanthal fences and the hamlet are kurinji's

comparisons.tenor: the girl's broad shoulders, as bamboo

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the companion is inferred; the colophon names only the speaker; the addressee is inferred from the poem

links.note: Both use the saying 'eating one's own in one's own house': Kural 1107 for the joy of the beloved's embrace, Kuruntokai 83 for jackfruit hanging sweet on the lover's own hill as the mother announces he will come.
links.teaches: The pair shows the phrase was a common measure of untroubled, owned pleasure; the Kural applies it to union itself, while the Kuruntokai friend lays it on the lover's land at the moment marriage is promised, so the image belongs to the settled household rather than to secret love.

links.note: In Kural 1168 the woman says the night that lulls every creature to sleep has only her for company; in Kuruntokai 86 she asks at midnight whether anyone else hears the cow's bell.
links.teaches: The Kural asserts that she alone is awake; the Kuruntokai poem tests the claim with a question and finds one other wakeful thing, a lonely cow whose bell rings with her, so the solitude the Kural states is shown as a search for a companion.

links.note: Kural 1188: people say she has paled, no one says he left her. Kuruntokai 87: the god destroys the false, my lover is not false, yet my brow has paled.
links.teaches: Read together they show why the blame lands on her body: in the Kuruntokai the woman herself clears him before the avenging god, so the only visible sign of the wrong is her pallor, which is exactly the one-sided verdict the Kural's woman complains of.

links.note: Both compare a hill girl to the figure carved on Kolli's western face; 89 calls Kolli Porayan's, 100 calls it Ori's.
links.teaches: The same carved figure serves two poets as the measure of a girl's innocence while the hill is credited to different lords, the Chera Porayan and the archer Ori, so the simile was fixed to the place and outlived the change of its master.

links.note: Avvaiyar's Purananuru 97 warns Anji's enemies that his worn swords, spears and elephants prove resistance is hopeless; her Kuruntokai 91 makes the night terror of a frontier town fearing Anji the measure of a wife's sleepless marriage.
links.teaches: The same poet supplies both sides of Anji's war: the puram poem speaks for the conqueror's threat, the akam poem borrows the sleeplessness of the threatened town, showing that the fear puram praise produces was available to akam as an image of domestic misery.

links.note: Kural 1222 asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard-hearted as hers; Kuruntokai 92 at sunset watches birds hurry home with food for their young.
links.teaches: The Kural guesses that the evening suffers from a cruel partner like hers; the Kuruntokai's dusk answers that every creature in it is hurrying home to its own, so the hard-heartedness is her man's alone and not the hour's.

links.note: Kural 1308: what use is suffering where there is no lover who knows you suffer; Kuruntokai 93: what is sulking worth when love is gone; do not speak against him, he is mother and father to us.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the reasoning that sulking needs a lover who will notice; the Kuruntokai wife draws the conclusion in her own case and adds the reason she cannot quarrel, her total dependence on him, so the maxim is shown ending in silence rather than in oodal.

links.note: Kural 1088: my might, feared in battle, broke before her bright brow; Kuruntokai 95: her grace like water quenched my strength like fire.
links.teaches: The Kural reports the man's defeat as a wonder of scale, so great a strength and so small a brow; the Kuruntokai explains it by kind, water putting out fire, so his strength was not outmatched but met by its natural undoing.

links.note: On the Kural reading where gossip feeds love and keeps it from drooping, Kuruntokai 97 disagrees: the secret turned to talk in the square is one of four things scattered apart, with her beauty lost and the man in his own town.
links.teaches: The man in the Kural can welcome gossip as fuel for love, while the woman in the Kuruntokai counts it among her losses, so the pair shows that rumour's value in the akam world depends on which lover bears it.

source_issues: 81: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but the poem is all shore (கடல், கானல், ஞாழல், பெண்ணை); marked neythal.
84: line 5 is the repaired tamilvu reading, as show flags.
94: line 3 is the repaired tamilvu reading, as show flags.
81 and 85: the poet's name is spelt வடம வண்ணக்கண் in 81 and வடம வண்ணக்கன் in 85; the colophons are copied as they stand.
